w:r.w:t: Flooding in urban areas is closely linked to inadequate drainage infrastructure, yet existing geospatial data in Shapefile format remains inaccessible to non-specialist stakeholders due to the complexity of conventional GIS software [1]. This paper presents B-DRAIN (Bekasi Drainage Information Network), a web-based

that integrates interactive spatial visualization with spatial analysis capabilities for flood-prone areas and drainage infrastructure in Bekasi City, Indonesia. The system is developed using a Software Development Life Cycle (SDLC) methodology, combining a React.js and Leaflet.js frontend with
-format spatial data sourced from the National Geospatial Information Agency (BIG) at 1:25,000

, BPBD Kota Bekasi, and OpenStreetMap [10][11][12][14]. B-DRAIN provides three core spatial analysis modules: buffer analysis to assess drainage coverage around flood points, proximity analysis to measure distance from flood incidents to nearest drainage segments, and a priority scoring system to identify areas requiring urgent infrastructure improvement. Functional testing across all 15 system features confirms correct operation of layer visualization, spatial filtering, measurement tools, and analysis modules. The system demonstrates that open-source web GIS technology can effectively provide accessible, interactive spatial decision support for urban flood mitigation stakeholders without requiring specialized GIS software.

Urban flooding is one of the most persistent natural disaster challenges in Indonesian cities, driven by a combination of high rainfall intensity, rapid urbanization, and insufficient drainage capacity [1]. Bekasi City, located in West Java Province and home to over 3.5 million inhabitants, consistently ranks among the most flood-affected urban areas in the country [1][3]. Flood events recur annually across multiple sub-districts (
), causing property damage, traffic disruption, and casualties that disproportionately affect densely populated residential areas [3][14].

A. Web-Based GIS for Flood Management

Web GIS platforms have been increasingly adopted to support disaster risk reduction by making spatial data accessible through web browsers without requiring dedicated client software [7]. Pradhan and Lee demonstrated the application of GIS-based spatial analysis for flood susceptibility mapping using frequency ratio and logistic regression models integrated within a web interface, establishing that accessible web-based tools significantly improve stakeholder engagement with spatial hazard data [2].
et al. further showed that integrating multiple spatial datasets — particularly drainage network data alongside topographic and land-use layers — substantially improves
flood risk zone delineation accuracy compared to single-source approaches [4].
In Indonesia, BNPB's national hazard information platform and BPBD's regional systems have adopted

frameworks for real-time disaster monitoring and reporting [3][14]. However, these platforms focus primarily on data dissemination and notification, with limited capabilities for user-driven spatial querying, layer comparison, or proximity-based analysis that operational infrastructure managers require [3][6].

The Geoportal Kota Bekasi provides city-level spatial data access including administrative boundaries and infrastructure layers, while the Ina-Geoportal (BIG) provides national topographic basemaps at scales up to 1:25,000 [12][13]. Neither platform provides an integrated analytical interface combining flood incident data with drainage infrastructure analysis, creating the gap this research addresses.
B. Spatial Analysis Methods for Flood Risk

Buffer analysis and proximity analysis are well-established GIS methods for quantifying the spatial relationship between hazard locations and surrounding infrastructure [5]. Costache et al. applied spatial proximity metrics to evaluate the relationship between water network density and flash flood susceptibility, finding that distance to drainage features is among the most significant predictors of inundation risk and should be a primary criterion in flood vulnerability assessments [5].

Priority scoring frameworks combining multiple spatial indicators — including flood frequency, event severity, and infrastructure coverage — have been applied in urban flood management contexts to provide municipalities with objective, quantitative justification for infrastructure investment prioritization [6]. Hussain et al. demonstrated that composite spatial scoring approaches outperform single-indicator rankings in matching expert assessments of flood intervention urgency [6].
C. Open-Source Technologies for Web GIS
Leaflet.js has established itself as the leading open-source JavaScript library for interactive web mapping [7]. Its lightweight architecture (~42 KB core), extensive plugin ecosystem, and native

support make it particularly effective for web GIS applications targeting non-specialist users who require fast load times and intuitive interaction without sacrificing geospatial functionality [7]. The combination of React.js component architecture with Leaflet.js has been shown to enable modular, maintainable web GIS applications with scalable state management and responsive user interfaces [8].

OpenStreetMap provides openly licensed, community-maintained geospatial data including drainage infrastructure (waterways, channels, culverts) that is particularly valuable where official drainage network datasets are unavailable or not publicly accessible [11].

B-DRAIN was successfully implemented as a web-based GIS application accessible through a standard browser. The system architecture, illustrated in Fig. 1, comprises three components: (1) the React/Leaflet frontend responsible for map rendering and user interaction; (2) the Flask REST API backend providing the ML prediction endpoint; and (3) the static GeoJSON data layer served via Vite. The frontend communicates with the backend exclusively through CORS-enabled REST API calls, ensuring clean separation of concerns and independent deployability of each component.
The system successfully renders all eleven spatial datasets as interactive Leaflet layers, with layer toggling controls in the sidebar. Administrative boundaries (

) are rendered as choropleth layers with flood risk scoring overlays. Flood inundation zones are displayed with semi-transparent fill to allow base map context visibility. Drainage network polylines are rendered with width variation by channel order. The map supports zoom levels 10–18 with tile rendering via OpenStreetMap.

The buffer analysis function generates overlay zones at four configurable radii. In representative test cases, the 500 m buffer around primary drainage channels in Bekasi Utara sub-district encompassed approximately 23% of the total sub-district area, while the 1000 m buffer covered 61%. Proximity analysis results indicate that the average distance from residential
centroids to the nearest primary drainage channel is 847 m, with a range of 112 m (Bekasi Selatan) to 2,340 m (
Gede). Priority scoring classified 4 of 12 sub-districts as high priority (score > 0.70), 6 as medium priority (0.40–0.70), and 2 as low priority (< 0.40).

B-DRAIN demonstrates that open-source web GIS technologies can effectively support flood risk

communication in an Indonesian urban context. The system fulfills all stated functional requirements, achieving a 100% pass rate in functional testing. The spatial analysis functions provide actionable insights

urban planning: buffer analysis identifies exposure zones around drainage infrastructure, proximity analysis quantifies accessibility of drainage services, and priority scoring enables comparative risk assessment across sub-districts.

The machine learning component validation reveals both the potential and limitations of data-driven flood risk classification at the sub-district scale. The 81.56% accuracy and 0.7067 macro F1-score are competitive for the three-class, 212-instance dataset, but can be improved with larger, higher-resolution training data. Future work should incorporate real-time sensor data (rainfall gauges, water level sensors) to enable dynamic risk updating. Integration with the Indonesian National Disaster Management Agency (BNPB) data infrastructure would further enhance data currency and spatial coverage.

This paper presented B-DRAIN, a web-based Geographic Information System for flood risk spatial analysis in Bekasi City, Indonesia. The system integrates eleven multi-source spatial datasets, three spatial analysis methods (buffer, proximity, priority scoring), and a Gradient Boosting machine learning classifier within a React/Leaflet.js frontend served by a Flask REST API backend. Key findings are: (1) the system successfully renders and queries all spatial datasets with sub-second response times for spatial analysis operations; (2) functional testing confirms 100% pass rate across 15 test cases; (3) the Gradient Boosting classifier achieves a test macro F1-score of 0.69, with particularly strong performance on the high-risk class (F1 = 0.86); (4) the confusion matrix confirms that critical cross-class errors (
) are minimal, comprising only 2 of 43 test instances.

The research demonstrates the feasibility of low-cost, open-source web GIS for urban flood risk management in developing-country contexts, where institutional GIS capacity may be limited. B-DRAIN provides a replicable framework that can be adapted to other Indonesian cities with comparable data availability. Future work will focus on real-time data integration, mobile-native deployment, and expansion of the training dataset to improve minority-class classification performance.
